title: Deep sea observation station that tracks climate change set to be pulled from Gulf of Alaska
text:
Ocean Station Papa, which collects ocean and climate data, is one of five federal ocean monitoring stations the National Science Foundation plans to dismantle over the next couple of years.
Researchers recover an old mooring from Ocean Station Papa during an Ocean Observatories Initiative expedition. The National Science Foundation plans to yank a long-standing ocean observation station from the sea floor far off the coast of Alaska next year.is located more than 2.5 miles beneath the water’s surface in the Gulf of Alaska.
It’s made up of three large, round moorings arranged in a triangle and equipped with Russ Hopcroft, chair of the oceanography department at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, said its removal could make it harder to study ocean warming events like a combined marine heatwave and El Niño that “It’s an unfortunate time to have something being pulled out of the water with all these predictions we’re hearing about this super El Niño coming, and this is, you know, one of the important sentinel sensors in that system,” Hopcroft said.data sets in the North Pacific.
Papa is anchored to the ocean’s bottom in the middle of a rotating current system called the Alaska Gyre, which is a major driver of regional weather. The gyre also influences fisheries and ocean acidification, since it forces deep, nutrient and carbon-rich offshore waters to the surface in a process called upwelling.
“The advantage of having a mooring like that out there is you get all that high-resolution data, not just at the surface, but through the whole water column,” Hopcroft said. Seth Danielson is an oceanography professor at the University of Alaska Fairbanks who studied the heatwave. He said he couldn’t have done that without measurements of deep ocean temperatures.
“We wouldn’t have been able to know how much heat actually was in the ocean during the time of the blob,” he said. The University of Alaska operates other ocean floor stations closer to shore, but Danielson said none are as far out at sea as Papa.
In addition to tracking ocean temperature, he said Papa tracks salinity, pressure, water chemistry and nutrient concentrations. He said that’s important for fisheries managers who look at long-term ocean conditions when planning catch limits for fisheries in the Gulf of Alaska.
“Ocean Station Papa is just one of those key sites that has consistent data that stretches over many decades,” Danielson said. Mike England, a spokesperson for the National Science Foundation, said in an email to KTOO that the federal government isn’t cancelling the Ocean Observatories Initiative, but scaling back the program is part of the foundation’s wider strategy of a “nimbler approach to prioritize support for evolving scientific priorities.
” It’s unclear how the initiative will operate once the foundation pulls all of its stations out of the ocean over the next couple of years. Image from work supported by the National Science Foundation Ocean Observatories Initiative, a major facility fully funded by the NSF.

NSF to Dismantle Deep-Ocean Monitoring System Amid Climate Tracking ConcernsThe National Science Foundation announced plans to dismantle the Ocean Observatories Initiative, a $368 million deep-ocean monitoring system that for years had helped researchers understand climate impacts. The project, which collects data on temperatures, currents, and the ocean's absorption of carbon dioxide, involves removing more than 900 instruments. Scientists interpret this as the Trump administration's latest effort to stop climate tracking. The data from the initiative, particularly from the Irminger Sea, has been crucial for studying the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Current (AMOC), a system that scientists fear is weakening due to planetary heating and could collapse, causing major global weather changes. The NSF claims the dismantling will help prioritize support for evolving scientific priorities and emerging technologies, while critics argue that tracking ocean currents and temperatures is essential for understanding climate tipping points and their effects on everything from fishing to hurricanes.
